role: independent primary-source applicability adjudicator for one Planning candidate
candidate: During ordinary Planning using only the original cosmic deck and no alien/card exception, the main players cannot agree who must commit their encounter card first and keep changing choices. Who must commit first, who may still choose afterward, and may offense change its commitment again?
disposition_meaning: Do not adopt the offense-first / defense-may-decide / offense-cannot-change answer as a source-established answer to this original-cosmic-only question. The inspected primary text establishes that answer for the stated mixed cosmic/reward-card dispute; it does not positively establish the extension. This is not a finding that an opposite original-only sequence is mandated.

scope.included: Original 2008 CE01 base game, original 50 aliens, general flares, and base-relevant material in the 2018 official FAQ.

exact_source_question_answer_meaning.question_trigger: Both main players keep switching between cosmic and reward deck cards during Planning. The answer addresses that named dispute when they cannot agree.
operative_sequence: Offense must commit their encounter card first.
Defense may then decide which type of encounter card to play.
Offense can no longer change their mind.
exact_source_question_answer_meaning.context: The item is under Expansion-Specific Questions / Cosmic Incursion / Reward Deck on FAQ page 8. The entire Reward Deck section, from character 38203 through the page-8 end before Rift Questions (which begins at 40715 on page 9), was visible within inspected ranges. Its neighboring entries discuss cosmic-versus-reward deck references, reward sources, public card backs, separate discard piles, and random selection across both backs.
exact_source_question_answer_meaning.wording_limit: The answer does not say that every original-only Planning dispute uses this sequence. Its conditional opening, If both players cannot agree, has the mixed-deck dispute in the question as its immediate antecedent. The phrase which type appears within that context; it is not an explicit all-Planning scope declaration.
exact_source_question_answer_meaning.location_caveat: The expansion heading is contextual evidence, not an automatic exclusion test. For example, the neighboring definition that the deck means the cosmic deck unless otherwise stated can independently describe original-deck card references. Each item still requires its own applicability analysis.

established: The base Planning rule requires offense and defense each to select an encounter card from hand and place it facedown.
A base-only card-selection state exists. The page-10 Zombie/Clone example has both players play encounter cards facedown, then reveal them.
Base Reveal explicitly makes turning cards faceup simultaneous. That does not explicitly make selection simultaneous or prescribe a forced commitment sequence.
positive_original_base_enabler.not_established: Neither the original Planning instruction nor that example states who must choose first in a deadlock, grants a response choice after the other commits, or supplies the FAQ no-offense-change instruction. Existence of the base-only state supplies no positive bridge from the mixed-deck FAQ item.

actual_rule_text_versus_extrapolation.actual_rules: The base says each selects and places facedown. The FAQ gives a mandatory commitment sequence in the question that explicitly involves switching between two deck origins.
actual_rule_text_versus_extrapolation.proposed_extrapolation: Removing cosmic/reward switching from that question and applying the same mandatory sequence to repeated selection changes among original cosmic-deck cards requires an additional scope inference.
actual_rule_text_versus_extrapolation.source_support_assessment: No inspected source clause expressly makes that transfer, cross-references ordinary Planning to this FAQ item, or declares a universal encounter-card commitment deadlock rule. A similar procedural problem is not itself textual authority.
actual_rule_text_versus_extrapolation.not_an_inverse_rule: Failure to establish this extension does not establish defense-first, simultaneous commitment, unrestricted changes, or a table procedure. None is selected here.

generic_timing_and_alien_priority.analysis: The detailed page-12 rule describes a timing conflict as two players invoking contradictory special effects simultaneously and orders resolution offense, defense, then other players clockwise from offense. The page-16 summary orders effects without restating that definition. Ordinary indecision over choosing a facedown encounter card, with no alien/card exception, is not positively identified as such a special-effect conflict. Even a broader offense-priority reading alone would not state the defense-after-commit and irrevocable-offense details.

The general FAQ says to finish an effect before another and to use Timing Rules when two things should happen simultaneously. It also puts unassociated effects last. These are real general instructions, but neither identifies the candidate choice deadlock as two simultaneous effects nor defines card commitment or its reversibility. Applying them here to obtain the whole FAQ answer would require interpretation.

An alien power takes precedence over conflicting game rules. The original Oracle/Sorcerer example derives its sequence from the powers specifying before selection and after both selections. It demonstrates that explicit alien text can order choices. The candidate excludes such exceptions; this example supplies no ordinary commitment order.

The general FAQ permits changing a decision about invoking a power or effect after another action or timing outcome changes the game state, illustrated by Trader/Visionary. It is not an express permission or prohibition about replacing an ordinary encounter-card commitment, and it does not make the mixed-deck no-change clause universal.

The immediately preceding kicker item has a similar offense-first fallback when players cannot decide, but it expressly concerns kickers, which are excluded here. Similarity supports a possible design interpretation, not an independently stated original-only rule.

irreducible_ambiguity.question: Did the FAQ authors intend their mixed-deck answer also to express a universal Planning deadlock procedure?
irreducible_ambiguity.assessment: The sources can support that as an analogy, but do not positively resolve it. The immediate question and the surrounding public-backs rules support reading the issued ruling as addressing the mixed-deck case. The answer does not expressly say only in that case, so absolute exclusion of every intended broader application would also overclaim. The defensible boundary is the expressly established case; the extension remains underdetermined.
irreducible_ambiguity.consequence: Defer this proposed original-only procedural question as a source-keyed item rather than inventing a table ruling.

alternative_source_exact_statements.statement: During Planning, offense and defense each select an encounter card (attack, negotiate, or morph) from hand and place it facedown. During Reveal they turn those cards faceup simultaneously.
alternative_source_exact_statements.limit: Does not answer which player must commit first or whether a selected card may be changed.

alternative_source_exact_statements.scope: mixed cosmic/reward decks; outside candidate scope
alternative_source_exact_statements.statement: When both main players keep switching between cosmic and reward deck encounter cards during Planning and cannot agree, offense commits first; defense may then decide which type to play, and offense cannot change their mind.
alternative_source_exact_statements.limit: Preserve the explicit mixed-deck premise. Do not present this reformulation as an in-scope original-only rule.

faq_reward_question_answer.exact_text:
Q: Which main player must commit an encounter card when both main 
players keep switching between cosmic and reward deck cards during 
planning phase?
A: If both players cannot agree, the offense must commit their 
encounter card first, and then the defense may decide which type 
of encounter card to play (and the offense can no longer change 
their mind).

faq_reward_section_opening.exact_text:
Reward Deck
Q: Does any reference to “the deck” or “the discard pile” on any card 
exclude the reward deck/discard pile?
A: “The deck” always refers to the cosmic deck, and “the discard 
pile” always refers to the cosmic deck discard pile, unless 
otherwise stated.

faq_card_backs_public.exact_text:
Q. Are players ever allowed to hide the design of a card back from other 
players?
A: No.

faq_reward_random_selection.exact_text:
Q: How do you choose cards “at random” when both cosmic and reward 
cards are involved?
A: Players are allowed to see which card backs they are selecting. In 
essence,”at random” means “without seeing the faces of the cards.”

faq_kicker_commitment.exact_text:
Q. Is either main player required to commit to using or not using a 
kicker before the other main player decides about kickers? 
A: Either main player may change their mind, but if they cannot 
ultimately decide, the offense must commit first.

base_planning.exact_text:
5. Planning
The offense and the defense now each select an encounter card
from their hand (an attack, negotiate, or morph) and place it
facedown in front of themselves. If the defense has no encoun-
ter cards in hand, he or she may reveal any remaining cards
in hand, discard them, and then draw a new eight-card hand
before selecting a card during this phase. If the offense has no
encounter cards in hand, his or her turn ends immediately, as
described under “Drawing New Cards” on page 13.

base_reveal.exact_text:
6. Reveal
The offense and defense turn their cards faceup simultaneously
and a winner is determined.

base_example.exact_text:
Example: The Zombie (green) is the offense and has drawn a
destiny card instructing him to attack the Clone (red). He places
four ships in the hyperspace gate and points it at one of the Clone’s
planets that contains two defending Clone ships. The Zombie asks
both the Oracle (yellow) and the Sorcerer (blue) to be offensive
allies. The Clone asks only the Oracle to be a defensive ally. The
Oracle (to the left of the Zombie) has two offers. She chooses to ally
with the Clone and places two ships next to Clone’s planet, but not
on it (bringing the total to four). The Sorcerer allies with the Zom-
bie, adding two ships to the hyperspace gate (bringing the total to
six). Both the Zombie and Clone play encounter cards facedown,
then reveal them. The Zombie plays an attack card with a value
of 10. Added to the ships on his side, he has a total attack value of
16. The Clone is defending with four total ships but plays a card
with an attack value of 15, bringing his total to 19. The Clone
wins, keeping the Zombie off his planet.

base_timing_conflicts.exact_text:
Timing
Conflicts
The timing strip along the bottom of each alien sheet and all
non-encounter cards generally states when the component’s
game effect may be used. However, if there is still a timing
conflict (when two players invoke contradictory special effects
simultaneously) between powers, artifacts, and other game
items and effects, resolution takes place in the following order:
The offense.
1.
The defense.
2.
Players who are not the main players, starting with the
3.
player to the left of the offense and proceeding clockwise.

base_quick_reference_timing.exact_text:
Timing Conflicts
When timing conflicts occur, resolve effects in the
following order:
The offense.
1.
The defense.
2.
Players who are not the main players, starting
3.
with the player to the left of the offense and
proceeding clockwise.

base_alien_priority.exact_text:
Alien Powers and
Rules Conflicts
Each player has an alien power that allows him or her to break
certain game rules. In any case where game rules conflict with
an alien power, the power takes precedence.

base_alien_interaction.exact_text:
Alien Interactions
There are many ways for the different alien pow-
ers to interact, and sometimes players will need to
carefully examine the powers involved to deter-
mine this interaction. As an example, imagine an
encounter between the Oracle and the Sorcerer.
Looking at their alien sheets, it can be seen that
although both powers occur in the same phase,
the Oracle’s power to foresee takes place before
the Oracle selects a card, while the Sorcerer’s
power of magic takes place after both players have
selected a card. So, the Oracle’s power is used
first, forcing the Sorcerer to play his encounter
card faceup. The Oracle then looks at that card
and selects her encounter card, playing it face-
down. Now that both encounter cards have been
selected, the Sorcerer’s power may be used. If the
Sorcerer wishes, he may switch encounter cards
with the Oracle before revealing the Oracle’s card.
Of course, the Oracle knew that before he played
his card, so does the Sorceerer choose the card in
front of him or not?
So, if an alien interaction seems like it doesn’t
work, take a moment to carefully work through
the powers involved, and in almost all cases, the
interaction should become clear.

faq_interrupt_and_timing.exact_text:
Q: Can you always interrupt an effect to do something else? As an 
example, playing a flare in response to compensation, or an effect like 
a Finder artifact?
A: Other than playing a Zap of some kind, or an effect that 
specifically allows you to interrupt an action, no. You must 
complete an effect before executing another one. When two 
things should happen simultaneously, use the Timing Rules. Keep 
in mind, a subseqent effect could still undo the original effect.

faq_changed_mind_about_power.exact_text:
Q: Can a player change their mind about invoking a power or effect if 
somone else’s action or timing rule outcome changes the game state? As 
an example, Trader attempts to trade hands with Visionary, but since 
both aliens use their powers in the same phase, and Visionary is 
offense, he wishes to use their power first to force Trader to play an 
attack 04 (knowing Trader will get Visionary’s attack 04 if they trade 
hands). Can Trader decide to not trade hands at this point?
A: Yes.

faq_unassociated_effects.exact_text:
Q: Where in the Timing Rules do affects not associated with any player 
fall (for example, the Black Hole hazard)?
A: Those are last, after players who are not main players, clockwise 
from the offense.

inspection_limitations: No summaries, snapshots, questionbanks, keys, maps, reader answers, grades, peer reviews/findings, canonical artifacts, outside websites, or community practice were consulted.
Only the two allowed extracted primary sources were inspected. Their PDFs were not needed to resolve extraction context and were not opened.

Keyword scans displayed isolated matching lines throughout both files, including incidental out-of-scope material. Those fragments and broad chunk edges are recorded in receipts; incidental expansion and Technology material was not used as authority for the candidate.

Complete relevant Planning passages, detailed and summary timing guidance, alien-priority and Oracle/Sorcerer guidance, the general FAQ block, and the complete Reward Deck section were visible. This is partial source coverage, not a full-file audit.

A final base-rule check included Drawing New Cards, Card Types, artifact, reinforcement, and complete flare-use guidance through its page-14 end. Those passages add no ordinary encounter-card commitment order; no unrelated reinforcement adjudication is made. Adjacent variant text at the chunk edge is not used as authority.
no_additional_scope_claims: No complete-bank, summary coverage, source-audit PASS, or signoff claim. No finding on unrelated reinforcement/Negotiate, alien-reveal, Calculator, or Hate choices.

Keyword-hit lines were displayed with offsets and trailing whitespace stripped; their hashes authenticate the original ranges. Non-source metadata and locator-only output are not counted as source text coverage.
